title: Chronic Pruritus — Cause Decision Tree
subtitle: Itch lasting >6 weeks: dermatologic vs systemic vs neuropathic

steps.prompt: Chronic pruritus (>6 weeks). Primary skin lesions visible on exam?
steps.detail: Primary lesions include papules, vesicles, wheals, plaques arising de novo. Secondary lesions only (excoriations, prurigo nodules, lichen simplex chronicus) do not count as primary. Distinguishing primary vs secondary lesions is the pivotal first step (Yosipovitch 2018, PMID 29385376).

branches.label: No — skin normal or only secondary lesions
Urticarial plaques/vesicles + tense bullae in older adult

steps.prompt: Atopic history vs well-demarcated silvery plaques on extensor surfaces?

branches.label: Atopic history, flexural, relapsing — Atopic Dermatitis

steps.detail: Manage per severity: topical steroids + emollients for mild-moderate; dupilumab (IL-4Rα biologic) or JAK inhibitors (upadacitinib, abrocitinib) for moderate-severe. Address itch directly with topical calcineurin inhibitors, crisaborole, or systemic therapies.
Itch is prominent in 60-90% of psoriasis patients. PASI assessment guides therapy. Biologics (IL-17A, IL-23, TNF inhibitors) address both inflammation and pruritus. Screen for psoriatic arthritis.
Patch testing for allergic contact; identify and eliminate offending allergen or irritant. Topical steroids for acute flares. Occupational dermatitis requires workplace modification.

Chronic urticaria (>6 weeks): 85% idiopathic/autoimmune. Tier 1: non-sedating H1 antihistamine (up to 4× standard dose). Tier 2: omalizumab (anti-IgE). Tier 3: cyclosporine. Screen for thyroid peroxidase antibody, CBC, CRP.

Sarcoptes scabiei var hominis. Treat entire household simultaneously. Permethrin 5% cream (preferred) or oral ivermectin 200 mcg/kg × 2 doses (1 week apart). Wash bedding/clothing. Post-scabetic itch may persist 2-4 weeks after cure — treat symptomatically; do not re-treat without evidence of re-infection.

6Ps: Pruritic, Purple, Polygonal, Planar, Papules, Plaques. Mucous membrane involvement in 50%. Topical class I steroid or tacrolimus first-line. Systemic options: acitretin, hydroxychloroquine, cyclosporine for severe disease. Oral lichen planus — monitor for malignant transformation.

steps.prompt: Age >60 with urticarial lesions/tense bullae vs relapsing patches with blood smear abnormality?

branches.label: Tense bullae + eosinophilia in older adult — Bullous Pemphigoid
Persistent patches → plaques → tumors in older adult — Mycosis Fungoides

steps.detail: Pre-bullous BP may present with intense pruritus and urticarial plaques only. DIF: linear IgG + C3 at BMZ. BP180/BP230 ELISA. First-line: superpotent topical steroid (Class I) + doxycycline (anti-inflammatory). Severe: systemic prednisone ± rituximab or omalizumab.

Most common cutaneous T-cell lymphoma. May itch intensely for years before diagnosis. Patch → plaque → tumor stage. Skin-directed therapy for early disease (NB-UVB, PUVA, topical mechlorethamine). Pruritus management: antihistamines, mirtazapine, gabapentin, aprepitant (NK1 antagonist).

Darier sign (urtication with stroking). Serum tryptase; bone marrow biopsy if systemic mastocytosis suspected. First-line: H1 + H2 antihistamines; cromolyn sodium; avoid triggers (NSAIDs, alcohol, heat, friction). KIT D816V mutation in systemic disease — midostaurin for advanced forms.

steps.prompt: Pruritus on normal/near-normal skin. Distribution and clinical clues?
steps.detail: When primary skin lesions are absent, a systematic approach by distribution and associated symptoms guides the diagnosis. Order tier-1 labs before subspecializing.

branches.label: Palms/soles, worse at night — cholestasis pattern
Generalized, patient on dialysis or with known CKD
Generalized + lymphadenopathy/B symptoms (fever, night sweats, weight loss)
Generalized, worse after warm shower (aquagenic pruritus)
Generalized in older adult, no findings, no systemic clues

steps.detail: Order: total bilirubin, direct bilirubin, ALP, GGT, AST/ALT, antimitochondrial antibody (AMA), abdominal ultrasound. Review all medications started within 4-12 weeks (drug-induced cholestasis). AMA+ → PBC. Alkaline cholestasis pattern without AMA → primary sclerosing cholangitis, intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy (if applicable), or drug-induced.

branches.label: Drug culprit identified (anabolic steroids, OCPs, antibiotics)

steps.detail: Palmar/plantar pruritus, worst at night. Ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) slows disease but may not relieve pruritus. Pruritus-specific: cholestyramine (first-line), rifampin, naltrexone, sertraline. Obeticholic acid + bezafibrate as second-line options. PMID 29385376.

Offending drug withdrawal is curative. Common culprits: anabolic steroids, oral contraceptives, chlorpromazine, amoxicillin-clavulanate, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. While awaiting resolution: cholestyramine, rifampin, or naltrexone for symptomatic relief.

Affects 40-70% of hemodialysis patients. Pathophysiology: uremic toxins, κ-opioid receptor dysregulation, small-fiber neuropathy. First-line: optimize dialysis adequacy + emollients + gabapentin/pregabalin (renally adjusted). Difelikefalin (κ-opioid agonist, IV post-dialysis) is FDA-approved for CKD-associated pruritus. Nalfurafine available in Japan/Korea. Capsaicin cream for localized areas. PMID 29385376.

Pruritus may precede Hodgkin lymphoma diagnosis by months to years. Order: CBC with differential (look for eosinophilia, Reed-Sternberg cells), LDH, ESR, CRP, uric acid. CT chest/abdomen/pelvis or PET-CT. Biopsy enlarged lymph node. Pruritus in Hodgkin is cytokine-mediated (IL-31, IL-6, thymus and activation-regulated chemokine [TARC]).

Pruritus resolves with effective chemotherapy (ABVD or BV-AVD regimen). While awaiting treatment: antihistamines, mirtazapine, gabapentin, aprepitant (NK1R antagonist). Pruritus is a systemic B symptom and a red flag that should not be attributed to skin disease alone. PMID 29385376.

Pruritus occurs in NHL, polycythemia vera, iron-deficiency anemia, and other hematologic conditions. Treat underlying disease. Symptomatic pruritus management: antihistamines, gabapentinoids, mirtazapine.

Aquagenic pruritus (intense burning/stinging/itching triggered within minutes of water contact at any temperature) is a hallmark of polycythemia vera (PV), occurring in 40-70% of patients. Check CBC: elevated hemoglobin/hematocrit + elevated RBC mass. JAK2 V617F mutation in 95% of PV. Management: phlebotomy + hydroxyurea + aspirin; interferon-α; ruxolitinib (JAK1/2 inhibitor) for refractory pruritus. PMID 29385376.

Malassezia-driven inflammatory condition. Ketoconazole 2% shampoo or ciclopirox shampoo + zinc pyrithione shampoo. For refractory scalp: low-potency topical steroid solution. Facial SD: ketoconazole cream or low-potency topical calcineurin inhibitor.
Treat with clobetasol shampoo or solution, tar shampoo, or calcipotriol/betamethasone foam. Biologic therapy if extensive or associated with plaque psoriasis.

Consider alopecia areata (itch in active disease), lichen planopilaris (burning itch + frontal fibrosing alopecia), seborrheic dermatitis-associated TE. Refer to dermatology for trichoscopy and possible scalp biopsy.

branches.label: Postmenopausal F or older M — lichen sclerosus pattern
Perianal only — consider pinworm (pediatric/adult), hemorrhoids, contact

steps.detail: Figure-of-eight distribution around vulva and perianal region in women; glans penis (BXO) in uncircumcised men. First-line: ultrapotent topical steroid (clobetasol propionate 0.05%) tapering over 3 months. Long-term maintenance. Biopsy to exclude dysplasia. 4-5% risk of squamous cell carcinoma — long-term follow-up mandatory.

Vulvovaginal candidiasis: fluconazole 150mg oral × 1 or topical azole. Bacterial vaginosis: metronidazole. Contact dermatitis: identify irritant/allergen. Patch testing if recurrent. Consider STI screening (trichomoniasis, herpes, syphilis) in sexually active patients.

Common causes: pinworm (Enterobius vermicularis — collect adhesive tape test at night), hemorrhoids, contact dermatitis (moist wipes, topical anesthetics), dietary irritants (coffee, spices). Treat underlying cause. Scotch tape test or stool O&P for pinworm; mebendazole 100mg × 1 if confirmed.

branches.label: Lateral forearm/dorsal arm (worse in summer, no rash)

steps.detail: Cervical radiculopathy (C5-C8) most common etiology; worsened by UV exposure. Ice pack test: relief with ice pack confirms neuropathic origin. MRI cervical spine. First-line: gabapentin/pregabalin, topical capsaicin 0.075%, sunscreen. Cervical traction or surgery if structural cause confirmed. PMID 29385376.

T2-T6 dorsal nerve entrapment. Hyperpigmented patch at medial scapular border is classic secondary change. First-line: topical capsaicin 0.025-0.075%, gabapentin/pregabalin, topical anesthetics. Physical therapy for paraspinal muscle release. Botulinum toxin injections in refractory cases. PMID 29385376.

Chronic itch in the site of prior herpes zoster, distinct from postherpetic neuralgia. Treat with topical capsaicin (including high-concentration 8% patch), lidocaine patches, gabapentinoids, or TCAs (amitriptyline). NMDA receptor antagonists (memantine) in refractory cases.

steps.prompt: Older adult with generalized itch + no systemic findings. Medications reviewed?

branches.label: Drug culprit identified (opioids, ACEi, statins, chemo)
No drug cause — dry skin in elderly

steps.detail: Common culprits: opioids (mu-receptor mediated; treat with nalbuphine or butorphanol), ACE inhibitors, statins, chloroquine, hydroxyurea, checkpoint inhibitors (pembrolizumab/nivolumab — often presents as maculopapular rash), targeted therapies (BRAF/MEK inhibitors). Discontinue if feasible; substitute alternative. PMID 29385376.

Most common cause of generalized pruritus in patients >65. Reduced epidermal lipids, impaired barrier function. Management: thick emollients BID (ceramide-containing preferred), short warm showers, humidifier. Symptomatic: low-dose naltrexone, gabapentin, or mirtazapine if emollients insufficient. Ensure TSH, CBC, CMP, ferritin normal to exclude systemic cause. PMID 29385376.
